purpose: Pentoxifylline helps improve blood flow through your body, especially to your legs and arms. It is mainly used to treat leg pain and cramping caused by poor circulation, a condition called intermittent claudication. It helps you walk farther and longer with less discomfort.
how_it_works: Your red blood cells normally need to be flexible to squeeze through small blood vessels. With poor circulation, these cells can become stiff and have trouble moving through tiny vessels. Pentoxifylline makes your red blood cells more flexible and also thins your blood slightly, so it flows more easily and delivers more oxygen to your muscles.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, upset stomach, vomiting, and dizziness. Some people also experience headache or flushing (feeling warm or red in the face). Taking the tablet with food can help reduce stomach upset.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have ever had a stroke, bleeding problems, or are allergic to caffeine or theophylline, as pentoxifylline is related to those medications. Avoid this medication if you have recently had bleeding in your brain or eyes. It can interact with blood thinners like warfarin, so your doctor may need to monitor you more closely. Do not crush or chew the extended-release tablets — swallow them whole.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 400 mg taken three times a day with meals. Your doctor may lower the dose to twice a day if you have kidney problems or experience side effects. It may take several weeks before you notice full improvement in your symptoms, so it is important to keep taking it as directed.
